text: Were it not for the lighthouse, many more ships would have been lost at sea.
tip: Start firmly on WERE, pause at the comma, and stress MAN-y MORE.

text: Rarely have I come across such a compelling argument.
tip: Stress RARE-ly at the start because the inversion is for emphasis. 'compelling' is com-PEL-ling.

text: The council's decision, controversial though it was, has largely been accepted.
tip: Drop your pitch slightly for 'controversial though it was'. Stress con-tro-VER-sial.

text: It's worth bearing in mind that first impressions aren't always accurate.
tip: 'bearing in mind' flows as 'bear-ring-in-mind'. AC-cu-rate is stressed on the first syllable.

text: She was on the verge of giving up when the breakthrough finally came.
tip: Link 'verge of' into 'ver-jov'. Stress BREAK-through.

text: Had we set off earlier, we might have avoided the worst of the traffic.
tip: 'Had we' replaces 'If we had', so stress HAD. 'might have' is /ˈmaɪtəv/.

text: The findings suggest that sleep plays a far greater role in memory than previously thought.
tip: Stress FAR GREAT-er, MEM-o-ry and PRE-vi-ous-ly. 'thought' is /θɔːt/.

text: What struck me most was the sheer generosity of the villagers.
tip: Cleft sentences save the weight for the end: stress SHEER and gen-er-OS-i-ty.

text: I can't help feeling that we've overlooked something rather important.
tip: Stress FEEL-ing, o-ver-LOOKED (ending in /t/) and im-POR-tant.

text: Not until the final chapter does the author reveal the thief's true identity.
tip: 'thief's' ends in /fs/. Stress NOT UN-til and i-DEN-ti-ty.

text: Whether or not the plan succeeds depends largely on the weather.
tip: In British English 'whether' and 'weather' sound the same: /ˈweðə/!

text: The dragon's hoard was rumoured to be worth a small fortune.
tip: 'hoard' /hɔːd/ and 'fortune' /ˈfɔːtʃuːn/ share /ɔː/, but 'worth' is /wɜːθ/.

text: Admittedly, the new library has its drawbacks, but on balance it's a vast improvement.
tip: Pause after 'Admittedly' and 'on balance'. 'vast' has a long British /ɑː/.

text: He's prone to exaggerating, so I'd take his story with a pinch of salt.
tip: ex-AG-ger-at-ing is /ɪɡˈzædʒəreɪtɪŋ/. Link 'pinch of' into 'pin-chov'.

text: So exhausted was the messenger that he collapsed at the castle gates.
tip: Stress SO ex-HAUST-ed. 'collapsed' ends in /pst/: /kəˈlæpst/.

text: The proposal, while ambitious, fails to address the underlying causes of the problem.
tip: Three chunks: The proposal | while ambitious | fails to address the underlying causes. The verb 'address' is ad-DRESS.

text: Little did she know that the old map would change her life completely.
tip: Stress LIT-tle and KNOW. com-PLETE-ly is stressed in the middle.

q: Is technology making us less sociable? Give a nuanced view using 'to some extent'.
model: To some extent it is, although it also helps us keep in touch with friends who live far away.
tip: Pause after the hedge 'To some extent' and stress ex-TENT.

q: Describe a challenge you overcame. Use a cleft sentence: 'What helped me most was…'.
model: What helped me most was having a friend who genuinely believed in me.
tip: Rise a little on 'most', pause, then stress the key idea at the end.

q: Why might a village have been abandoned? Speculate with 'might have', 'may have' or 'must have'.
model: The villagers might have left because the river dried up and the crops failed.
tip: 'might have' is /ˈmaɪtəv/. Keep 'have' weak and stress the reasons.

q: What would you change about your education? Begin with 'If I could go back'.
model: If I could go back, I would spend far more time learning languages.
tip: Pause after 'If I could go back'. 'I'd' counts as 'I would'.

q: Persuade the council to build a new park. Use 'Not only … but … also'.
model: Not only would a park improve people's health, but it would also bring the community together.
tip: After 'Not only' the verb comes first: 'Not only WOULD a park…'. Stress ON-ly and AL-so.

text: Seldom have I seen a goalkeeper make so many saves in a single match.
tip: Stress SEL-dom at the start, then let 'have I' be quick and light. Stress SAVES and SIN-gle.

text: The comet, visible only once every seventy-six years, lit up the night sky.
tip: Three chunks: The comet | visible only once every seventy-six years | lit up the night sky. Link 'lit up' into 'li-tup'.

text: Had it not been for the volunteers, the nature reserve would have closed years ago.
focus: Inversion: had it not been for
tip: Start firmly on HAD, pause at the comma, and stress vol-un-TEERS and CLOSED.

text: It was the robot's tiny solar panel that kept it running through the storm.
tip: Put the weight on the key idea: TI-ny SO-lar PAN-el. 'robot's' ends in /ts/.

text: The wind was so strong that we couldn't wind the kite string back in.
tip: The weather 'wind' is /wɪnd/, but to 'wind' a string is /waɪnd/. Same spelling, different sounds!

text: Considering how little training she'd had, her performance was remarkably assured.
tip: con-SID-er-ing, per-FOR-mance, re-MARK-ab-ly and as-SURED /əˈʃʊəd/. 'she'd had' is /ʃiːd hæd/.

text: The standing ovation for the school orchestra lasted several minutes.
tip: o-VA-tion is /əʊˈveɪʃn/. OR-ches-tra is stressed on the first syllable, and 'ch' sounds like /k/.

text: Bees, far from being a nuisance, are essential to the food we eat.
tip: Drop your pitch for 'far from being a nuisance'. NUI-sance is /ˈnjuːsns/ and es-SEN-tial is stressed in the middle.

text: The documentary shed light on how octopuses use tools to solve problems.
tip: To 'shed light on' something is to help us understand it. OC-to-pus-es is /ˈɒktəpʊsɪz/.

text: Whichever route you choose, allow plenty of time to reach the campsite before dark.
tip: 'allow' rhymes with 'cow' /əˈlaʊ/, but 'route' sounds like 'root' /ruːt/. Pause after 'choose'.

q: Should schools have longer breaks? Give a balanced view with 'While' and 'I'd argue that'.
model: While longer breaks mean less lesson time, I'd argue that they help us concentrate better afterwards.
tip: Pause after the 'While' part, then stress AR-gue and CON-cen-trate.

q: Describe an invention you couldn't live without. Use a cleft sentence: 'What I value most is…'.
model: What I value most is my bike, because it gives me the freedom to explore on my own.
tip: Rise a little on 'most', pause, then stress BIKE and FREE-dom.

q: Imagine your school had no rules for one day. Speculate with 'would probably' or 'might well'.
model: Some students would probably eat pudding first, but most of us might well miss the routine by lunchtime.
tip: 'might well' links smoothly /maɪt wel/. Stress PROB-ab-ly, WELL and rou-TINE.

q: How could your town protect wildlife? Use a passive with 'could be' or 'should be'.
keywords: could be|should be|might be|ought to be
model: More hedges could be planted along the roads, and street lights should be dimmed at night for bats.
tip: Keep 'be' weak /bi/ and stress the participles: PLANT-ed, DIMMED.

q: Tell me about a misunderstanding with a friend. Use 'It turned out that'.
model: I thought my friend was ignoring me, but it turned out that she simply hadn't heard me.
tip: Link 'turned out' into 'tur-ndout'. Pause just before it, then stress SIM-ply and HEARD.

q: Is it better to be brilliant at one sport or to try lots of them? Hedge with 'It depends on' or 'to a large extent'.
keywords: it depends|to a large extent|to some extent
model: It depends on the person, but trying lots of sports usually helps you find the one you love.
tip: Pause after 'It depends on the person,'. Stress de-PENDS and U-su-al-ly.

q: Recommend a book or series to a friend. Use 'If you're into…, you'll love…'.
model: If you're into mysteries, you'll love the Lighthouse Detectives, because every chapter ends with a twist.
tip: 'you're into' is /jɔːr ˈɪntə/ with a linking r. Stress LOVE and TWIST.

q: Persuade your class to join a beach clean-up. Use 'Imagine how' and 'we could'.
model: Imagine how proud we'd feel if we could fill twenty bags of rubbish in one morning!
tip: Say 'Imagine' with energy: i-MAG-ine. Let your voice rise with excitement on TWEN-ty BAGS.

text: Only after the third attempt did the paper rocket finally leave the ground.
tip: Stress ON-ly AF-ter and THIRD. Keep 'did the' light, and let 'leave the ground' flow.

text: The museum's dinosaur skeleton, believed to be the largest in Europe, attracts thousands of visitors.
tip: Three chunks: The museum's dinosaur skeleton | believed to be the largest in Europe | attracts thousands of visitors.

text: Should you spot a hedgehog in your garden, leave out a shallow dish of water.
tip: 'Should you' means 'If you'. Stress SPOT and HEDGE-hog. SHAL-low has a short /æ/.

text: The school band's first performance was, to put it mildly, a little out of tune.
focus: Comment phrases: to put it mildly
tip: Drop your pitch for 'to put it mildly', as if sharing a joke, then stress OUT of TUNE.

text: What fascinates me about owls is that they can turn their heads almost all the way round.
tip: Rise a little on 'owls', pause after 'is that', then stress TURN and ALL the WAY ROUND.

text: We'd barely put up the tent when the first drops of rain began to fall.
tip: Here 'We'd' means 'We had' /wiːd/. Link 'put up' into 'pu-tup'. Stress BARE-ly and RAIN.

text: Contrary to popular belief, goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds.
tip: CON-tra-ry is stressed first. Pause after 'belief', then contrast MONTHS and SEC-onds with strong stress.

text: The present she presented to the head teacher was a hand-painted mug.
tip: The noun PRES-ent /ˈpreznt/ is stressed first; the verb pre-SENT-ed /prɪˈzentɪd/ is stressed second. Same letters, different beats!

text: Exhausted but elated, the climbers reached the summit just before sunset.
tip: Pause after 'elated'. e-LA-ted is /ɪˈleɪtɪd/; SUM-mit and SUN-set are stressed on the first syllable.

text: The moment the bell rang, the corridor filled with chattering pupils.
tip: Pause after 'rang'. COR-ri-dor is stressed first, and the 'tt' in 'chattering' is a quick, light /t/.

q: Should all pupils learn a musical instrument? Use 'There's a strong case for'.
model: There's a strong case for it, because learning an instrument builds patience and confidence.
tip: Stress STRONG CASE, then pause before 'because'. PA-tience is /ˈpeɪʃns/.

q: Describe a book character you'd like to meet. Use 'What I admire about … is'.
model: What I admire about Matilda is that she stays brave and kind, even when the adults around her are unfair.
tip: Rise a little on the name, pause, then stress BRAVE and KIND.

q: How would you spend a day with no technology? Use 'I'd probably' and 'rather than'.
model: I'd probably go cycling with my friends rather than sitting at home feeling bored.
tip: 'I'd probably' is /aɪd ˈprɒbəbli/. Stress CY-cling and BORED.

q: What's one thing adults often misunderstand about young people? Use 'The thing is'.
model: Adults think we're always on our phones. The thing is, we often use them to learn new things.
tip: Pause after 'The thing is,'. Stress AL-ways and LEARN.

q: Talk about a time things didn't go to plan. Use 'Looking back'.
model: Our camping trip was rained off, but looking back, playing board games in the tent was the best part.
tip: Pause before and after 'looking back'. Link 'rained off' into 'rain-doff'.

q: Should school start later in the morning? Support your view with 'Research suggests that' or 'It's often said that'.
model: Research suggests that teenagers concentrate better later in the day, so a later start makes sense.
tip: re-SEARCH (or RE-search) and sug-GESTS. Stress LAT-er and SENSE.

q: Compare two hobbies you've tried. Use 'whereas' and 'far more'.
model: Swimming is relaxing, whereas rock climbing is far more exciting because every wall is a puzzle.
tip: Pause just before 'whereas' /weərˈæz/. Stress FAR MORE ex-CIT-ing.

q: Imagine you've won a trip anywhere in the world. Use 'I'd jump at the chance to'.
model: I'd jump at the chance to see the Great Barrier Reef before more of the coral disappears.
tip: To 'jump at the chance' is to accept eagerly. Link 'jump at' into 'jum-pat'.

q: Suggest a way to make lunchtime less noisy. Use 'One option would be to'.
model: One option would be to open the library at lunchtime for anyone who wants some peace and quiet.
tip: OP-tion is stressed first. Slow down for 'peace and quiet'.

q: Your friend wants to give up the piano. Give advice with 'If I were you' and 'at least'.
model: If I were you, I'd at least finish this term, because you might start enjoying it again.
tip: Keep your voice warm and gentle. Stress AT LEAST and a-GAIN.
